title: Grade-1 Fatty Liver: More Indians Are Developing It at Lower BMIs. What's Behind the Shift?
summary: Reports indicate that grade-1 fatty liver is increasingly seen in Indians with lower body mass indices than traditionally expected. Clinicians and public-health observers suggest a mix of factors — changing diets, central adiposity, sedentary lifestyles, and genetic predispositions — may be shifting risk to people who do not meet conventional overweight thresholds. The trend highlights the need for earlier screening and broader awareness of metabolic risk beyond BMI alone.

Grade-1 Fatty Liver: More Indians Are Developing It at Lower BMIs. What's Behind the Shift?

Across India clinicians are reporting a noticeable rise in cases of grade-1 fatty liver among people who do not appear overtly overweight by body mass index (BMI) standards. The pattern has prompted discussion among hepatologists, endocrinologists and public-health experts about whether traditional BMI cutoffs are sufficient to identify metabolic risk in the Indian population.

Experts point out several possible contributors. Changes in dietary patterns, including increased consumption of refined carbohydrates and processed foods, and a rise in sedentary behaviour are likely playing a role. Central adiposity — excess fat around the abdomen — can occur at lower overall BMI and is strongly linked to metabolic disturbances that promote fat accumulation in the liver. Genetic predisposition and insulin resistance are also cited as important factors that may explain why leaner individuals develop fatty liver disease.

The shift has practical implications for screening and prevention. Reliance on BMI alone may miss individuals at risk, so clinicians advocate for a more comprehensive assessment that includes waist circumference, blood tests for metabolic markers, and, where indicated, liver imaging. Public-health messaging that focuses exclusively on weight may need to broaden to emphasise diet quality, physical activity, and regular metabolic screening.

Awareness and early intervention are key to preventing progression from simple steatosis to more advanced liver disease. Lifestyle interventions — improved nutrition, increased physical activity and targeted management of diabetes and dyslipidaemia — remain the cornerstone of treatment. Policymakers and healthcare providers in India are being urged to update screening guidelines and increase community education to address this emerging pattern.
